purpose: A document is read by a person or an AI who comes to it for a purpose, at any time after it is written, in its own language or through a machine translation into theirs. Refactoring changes how the document says what it says, never what it says, and adds nothing: the reader takes in each sentence on first reading, reading once from the top only the parts their purpose needs.

checklist.what: Shown only a section's figure, before reading its text, can the reader explain to a colleague what the section tells?
checklist.why: If yes, the reader takes in who does what in what order, or how things relate, at a glance. The figure takes the place of the sentences that told the same, and the text under it holds only what it cannot show. A box names one thing and a line says what one does to another; a sentence in a box must be read. A section whose point is one sentence has that sentence in place of a figure. If no, the reader pieces the point together from sentences spread through paragraphs, and misses a step or gives it to the wrong one.
grounds: plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Use lists": lists "Help the reader understand the order in which things happen".
plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Use tables to make complex material easier to understand": "Tables help your audience see relationships that are often times hidden in dense text."
Google developer documentation style guide, "Highlights": "Use numbered lists for sequences."

examples.fails: A section that tells the booking flow in three paragraphs, then draws the same flow as five boxes, each holding two to six sentences. (A figure is there, but the reader must read every box, and reads the flow twice.)
examples.passes: The same section opens with a figure of the flow: the worker picks a room and a time, RoomBook asks the calendar, the room's owner approves a restricted room, RoomBook books it and emails the worker. Under it one sentence gives what the figure cannot: a restricted room waits up to a day for its owner.

checklist.what: After reading any sentence once, as written and again through a machine translation into their own language, such as Google Translate, can the reader say in each case who or what does what in it?
checklist.why: If yes, the reader takes in each sentence on first reading, in any language, and acts on what the writer meant. If no, a sentence that makes two points needs more than a few words, and one whose actor hides behind a passive verb or a noun made from a verb leaves the reader to guess who acts. A machine translator also guesses, and can guess wrong, where a sentence opens with its object, leaves out "that", "a" or "the", or has a "which" that can refer to two nouns; in Japanese, where a sentence has no subject or strings together several は, で or の. The sentence is reworded or split, not explained by another.
grounds: plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Use active voice": "Active voice makes it clear who is supposed to do what."
plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Write short sentences": "Express only one idea in each sentence."

Microsoft Writing Style Guide, "Writing tips" (Global communications), Additional tips for machine translation: "Writing style affects the quality of machine translation." and "Write sentences that use standard word order (that is, subject + verb + object) whenever possible."

Microsoft Writing Style Guide, "Writing tips" (Global communications), Tips for all global content: "Include that and who. They help to clarify the sentence structure." and "Articles help readers and translation software identify the nouns and modifiers in a sentence."
文化審議会「公用文作成の考え方（建議）」(2022), Ⅲ-3 ア: 「一文が長くなると、その構造は複雑になりやすい。」 and カ: 「接続助詞の「が」や中止法（述語の用言を連用形にして、文を切らずに続ける方法）を多用する書き方は避ける。」
文化審議会「公用文作成の考え方（建議）」(2022), Ⅲ-3 オ: 「省略されているかどうかにかかわらず、主語と述語の関係が明らかに分かるようにする。」 and シ: 「言葉の係り方によって複数の意味にとれる表現を避ける。」

examples.fails: The rooms the worker picks RoomBook checks against the calendar, and confirmation of the booking follows. (A machine translator makes it say that the worker picks RoomBook, and no one is said to confirm.)
examples.passes: RoomBook checks each room that the worker picks against the calendar. RoomBook confirms the booking once it finds the room free.

checklist.what: Each time the reader meets a name, can they tell rightly whether it names a thing they have already met, and which one?
checklist.why: If yes, the reader keeps one picture of each thing from start to end, and a machine translator gives each name one meaning throughout. If no, a reader who meets a second name for one thing takes it for a second thing, and a common word given a meaning of the document's own is read, and translated, with its usual meaning. One name is used for each thing everywhere; a synonym chosen to vary the writing is replaced, not explained.
grounds: plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Use the same terms consistently": "Using a different term may cause the reader to wonder if you're referring to the same group." and "You don't need to use synonyms to make your writing more interesting."
Google developer documentation style guide, "Write for a global audience", Use words in their primary sense: "Don't use the same word to mean different things."
ASD-STE100 (ASD), "About ASD-STE100": "In general, each word has only one meaning and is approved with only one part of speech."

examples.fails: Pick a room from the list. RoomBook holds your space for 15 minutes. (Is a space a room, or a desk?)
examples.passes: Pick a room from the list. RoomBook holds the room for you for 15 minutes.

checklist.what: When the reader meets a word they have not used themselves, can they tell what it means right where they meet it?
checklist.why: If yes, the reader reads on with the writer's meaning. If no, the reader guesses, and their picture differs from the writer's wherever the guess is wrong; a word the writer's team uses every day is still new to a reader who has not used it. An everyday word takes the term's place; a term the content keeps carries its meaning in a few everyday words where it first appears, and no sentence is added to explain it.
grounds: plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Avoid jargon": "writers often fail to realize that terms they know well may be difficult or meaningless to their audience."

plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Minimize definitions": "readers are likely to forget that you'd assigned some common word a new meaning, and when they come upon the word later in your document they assign the common meaning, rather than your specialized one."

examples.fails: RoomBook offers only rooms that pass the fit check. The fit check is RoomBook's test of a room against a meeting, which compares the seats and the equipment. (The term is explained, but by a sentence added where everyday words would do.)
examples.passes: RoomBook offers only rooms with a seat for each attendee and the equipment the meeting needs.

checklist.what: Reading from the top, can the reader tell from each heading and its first sentence what the section gives, and understand each sentence without turning back or jumping ahead?
checklist.why: If yes, the reader picks the sections their purpose needs, and each reason, word and step a sentence rests on comes before it, a rule's exceptions beside the rule. If no, a reader who cannot tell what a section gives reads it to find out, and one sent back or ahead loses their place or reads on with a guess. A sentence is moved to where it is needed; no summary, preview or signpost sentence is added.
grounds: plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Place the main idea before exceptions and conditions": "The audience must absorb the exception, then the rule, and then usually has to go back to grasp the relationship between the two."

plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Minimize cross-references": "They may also overtax your users' short-term memory." and "Be sure that the reference you insert clearly describes the referenced material."
Google developer documentation style guide, "Highlights": "Put conditions before instructions, not after."

plainlanguage.gov (GSA archive), "Have a topic sentence": "Don't make readers hold a lot of information in their heads before getting to the point." and "Readers should be able to get good general understanding of your document by skimming your topic sentences."
Microsoft Writing Style Guide, "Top 10 tips for Microsoft style and voice", Get to the point fast: "Lead with what's most important."

examples.fails: Select the room and press Book. Before this, you must connect your calendar, as Setup below explains.
examples.passes: First connect your calendar in Settings > Calendar. Then select the room and press Book.

checklist.what: Is each fact the document tells written in one place only, whether in this document, in a document read beside it, in a figure or in the work itself (code, output), with every other place linking to it?
checklist.why: If yes, the reader reads each fact once, and it cannot disagree with itself: a change made in its one place reaches every reader. If no, once one copy changes the two say different things, and the reader follows the one they read first. A sentence that retells what a figure draws or what code does is such a copy. Each copy gives way to a link.
grounds: Hunt and Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer (1999), DRY: "Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system."

examples.fails: The README's Booking says a room is held for 15 minutes while you confirm. Its Limits says a room you pick is held for 10 minutes. The architecture document says the hold is not yet decided.
examples.passes: The README's Booking says a room is held for 15 minutes while you confirm. Limits and the architecture document link to Booking for the hold.
